prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map separates the near shelf edges and people (bright) from the windows, walls, and rear store structure (dark), making the aisle geometry and foreground clearance clearer than in RGB. Across frames 1–2, a person stands roughly 1–2 m ahead and left of the camera wearer beside shelves; the shelving and products extend from within about 0.5–1 m at the lower edges to roughly 2–4 m ahead, while the windows are several metres behind them. In frames 3–5, the view turns right: the nearest shelf moves into the centre/right foreground, roughly 0.5–1.5 m away, and another person appears near its left side at about 1–2 m, with shelf objects generally closer than the background windows. Exact metre estimates are unreliable because the map provides relative rather than calibrated depth, bright halos blur object boundaries, and the final frame has a large black upper-right region with missing or invalid depth.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map identifies people, bottles, and a cup as separate instances, clarifying which small foreground shapes belong to distinct objects when RGB motion blur makes their boundaries hard to see. In frame 1, one person is about 1–2 m ahead-left and partly cut off below; in frame 2, bottles occupy the near shelf around the centre-left while two overlapping person masks lie roughly 1–2 m ahead-right, indicating substantial mutual occlusion. Frames 3–5 show bottle groups on shelves ahead/right, generally within about 0.5–2 m of the camera wearer and tens of centimetres apart, while person masks shift from the right side toward the centre/left as the camera turns; several people are only partly visible at frame edges or behind shelves. The masks do not reliably encode facing direction or metric distance, and repeated or overlapping person labels, merged silhouettes, missed products, and unstable bottle boundaries make counts and exact positions uncertain.
descriptions.pose: The pose map exposes a few visible body and hand keypoints that are difficult to isolate in the blurred RGB, especially raised arms and hands relative to nearby shelves. In frame 1, the person about 1–2 m ahead-left has an upper-body skeleton with one arm extending left and the other bent upward, while a separate small hand cluster lies above; the lower body is outside the mapped region or undetected. Frames 2–3 contain only sparse, fragmented keypoints near people roughly 1–2 m ahead, and frames 4–5 contain no usable pose, so facing direction, gaze toward the camera wearer, and most person-to-object distances cannot be established reliably from this map. The detected hands appear near shelf height and may be within the depicted people’s arm reach, but the map is too incomplete to confirm contact, the camera wearer’s own reach, occluded limbs, or approach and retreat beyond the camera’s rightward turn.
